concept: UC queue pair one-direction drop warm-up check
summary: A one-direction drop is a freshly created Apple Thunderbolt RDMA UC queue pair that delivers in one direction only. UC never reports a lost message, so the failure appears as a first bulk exchange that times out with no completions. The warm-up check proves both directions before real traffic.

facts.text: A one-direction drop is a freshly created Apple Thunderbolt RDMA UC queue pair that delivers in one direction only. UC never reports a lost message, so the failure appears as a first bulk exchange that times out with no completions. The warm-up check proves both directions before real traffic.
Order in ds4's setup: exchange RDMA info over TCP, move the pair to RTR and RTS, exchange a READY frame, then run the warm-up (skipped when `DS4_TP_DISABLE_RDMA_WARMUP` is set).
The warm message is full size (16384 bytes, the RDMA maximum message) because, per the source comment, "64 B warm messages pass on a fresh direction while the first 16 KB chunks are still dropped".

Each side posts exactly one full-size receive, then resends a tagged message until the peer confirms receipt over the control socket (`DS4_TP_FRAME_RDMA_WARM`); the attempt loop is 20 rounds on UC with a 0.1 s deadline each, and 1 round on RC.
Because "a dropped UC message never arrives late", once both sides have received the tagged message no stray warm-up message can later land in the receive queue.

A second barrier protects a different failure: on Apple's Thunderbolt RDMA, a UC send that reaches a queue pair with no receive posted is not just lost, that direction "stops delivering for good". So every sender waits for the peer's `DS4_TP_FRAME_RDMA_POSTED` word (one control-channel round trip) that its receives are posted before it posts sends.

On failure the warm-up sets `warm_failed` (UC only) and returns the error `tp rdma: warm-up failed after %d attempts (recv %d, peer %d)`; `ds4_tp_attach_slab` then prints `ds4-tp: <error>; recreating the queue pair (setup attempt N)` and calls the re-create function. Re-creation stops after setup attempt 3, so a run can build the queue pair at most four times.

Re-creation destroys the queue pair and the completion queue, builds a new completion queue (512 entries) and a new queue pair (1024 send and 1024 receive work requests), and gets a new queue pair number; the packet sequence number includes `setup_attempt * 0x1000`. Both ranks take the path together because the warm-up status exchange gives them the same outcome.
Success prints `ds4-tp: rdma warm-up ok (N attempt[s]), queue depth recv R send S`.
The source comment names two triggers: "right after a working run and after role swaps".

With a warm-up that succeeds only on a later attempt, the first attempts' messages are the dropped ones; the docs warn not to treat repeated handshake or RDMA timeouts as a pass merely because a retry works.
Setting `DS4_TP_DISABLE_RDMA_WARMUP` removes the proof, so a dead direction would surface later as a timeout in the first bulk round.
JACCL's `rdma.cpp` has no warm-up round, no posted-receive barrier and a fixed packet sequence number, so a queue pair with a dead direction would hang instead of being re-created.

Is the drop a driver fault or a protocol effect? The ds4 comments describe two separate observed behaviours (a fresh pair that drops one direction, and a pair that dies when a send precedes a posted receive) and treat both as driver behaviour of UC on Thunderbolt. No Apple source confirms either.
Whether macOS 27's reworked `libthunderboltrdma` removes the one-direction drop.
Whether the failure rate depends on the previous run's teardown, since the source ties it to "right after a working run".
ds4 runs its warm-up after the READY barrier unless `DS4_TP_DISABLE_RDMA_WARMUP` is set.
The warm-up message is 16384 bytes because 64-byte messages pass on a fresh dead direction while the first 16 KB chunks are still dropped.
ds4's warm-up gives UC 20 rounds of 0.1 s each and RC one round.
A dropped UC message never arrives late, so no stray warm-up message can reach the receive queue after both sides have received.
On Apple Thunderbolt RDMA, a UC send into a queue pair with no posted receive kills that direction permanently, so ds4 waits for the peer's "receives posted" frame before sending.
ds4 re-creates a failed queue pair up to three times, four builds in total.
Re-creation builds a new 512-entry completion queue and a new 1024/1024-work-request queue pair, with a new queue pair number and a packet sequence number offset by `setup_attempt * 0x1000`.
The log strings are `rdma warm-up ok (N attempts), queue depth recv R send S`, `warm-up failed after N attempts (recv a, peer b)` and `recreating the queue pair (setup attempt N)`.
JACCL's `rdma.cpp` has no warm-up or receives-posted barrier.
